name: Raw milk for height

lead: Raw milk for height is the practice of drinking unpasteurised milk in the hope of growing taller. Followers in some height-focused communities see it as a nutrient-dense food that supports growth and immunity.

The chain is nutrition: protein and other milk nutrients are supplied, growth is supported, and final height benefits. Reference sources report that populations eating more dairy and animal protein tend to be taller, without separating raw from pasteurised milk, and they report that heating does not substantially change milk's nutritional value. No study of raw milk and height was found.

paras: People drink it as a daily food, often alongside other nutrition-focused height routines, and usually start in the teen years while growth is still possible. Supporters source it from farms where it is legal. Any effect on height would show up over years of growth, not weeks.

The CDC and FDA recommend against raw milk because it can carry pathogens such as Listeria, Salmonella and E. coli, with the highest risk in young children, older adults, pregnancy and weakened immunity. Outbreaks are documented. Legal status varies by country and US state.

angle.text: Some height-focused communities drink raw milk to supply protein and nutrients for growth and end up taller. Dairy-rich diets track with taller populations in reference sources, but no study has looked at raw milk and height specifically.

lead: Raw milk for height is the practice of drinking unpasteurised milk in the hope of growing taller or filling out one's frame. It circulates in height-focused and looksmaxxing circles under slogans such as "Raw Milk + Healthy = Holy Height" and is usually bundled with primal, carnivore and raw-food diets that also feature raw eggs, liver and meat.[1][2][3] The appearance goal is straightforward: milk supplies protein, calcium, fat and fat-soluble vitamins, and adherents treat it as the most complete form of a growth-supporting food for people whose growth plates are still open.[4]

The idea sits on top of a real and much older discussion about dairy and stature. Reviews of children's studies report that habitual cow's milk intake is mostly linked to greater height or faster growth, with some observational studies finding no significant association, and Wikipedia's article on human height notes that populations eating more dairy and animal protein have tended to be taller.[5] That literature concerns milk in general; it does not separate raw from pasteurised milk. Height is also strongly heritable, at roughly 60 to 80 percent in twin studies, and growth typically ends in the late teens.

The raw-milk movement behind the practice has its own lineage: the dental researcher Weston A. Price's 1939 travel book on diet and facial development, the Primal Diet of Aajonus Vonderplanitz, the Weston A. Price Foundation founded in 1999 and the American "food freedom" campaigns over raw-milk access.[6][7][8] Proponents say raw milk tastes better, keeps more nutrients and supports immunity.[9] The CDC and FDA advise against drinking it because it can carry pathogens, a 2011 meta-analysis found that pasteurisation changes some vitamins but has a minimal effect on overall nutritive value, and legal access varies widely by country and US state.[9][10][11] No published study has measured height in people drinking raw versus pasteurised milk.

paras: Raw milk is milk sold or consumed without pasteurisation, the mild heat treatment that became standard in the twentieth century. Wikipedia reports that proponents credit it with better flavour, more nutrition, immune support and protection against allergies.[9] In looksmaxxing forums the milk is usually discussed alongside raw meat, liver and eggs as part of a primal-diet approach, and sometimes as a way to improve skin, hormones or bone structure.[2][3]

For height specifically, the reasoning offered by members runs along three lines. First, milk is a dense source of protein and calcium, nutrients needed for bone growth. Second, raw milk is said to retain enzymes, whey proteins and fats that heating alters, so it is seen as a fuller version of the food. Third, some posters mention growth hormone and related signalling that milk is thought to influence in the young.[4] One thread describes a member who did not drink much milk growing up and is still taller than his family by several inches, a data point that other members read as showing how much height depends on genetics.[4]

Wikipedia's article on human height notes that average national height correlates with protein quality, that populations with many cattle and high dairy intake were historically taller (citing the early nineteenth-century US, Argentina, New Zealand and Australia), and that malnutrition is linked to stunted growth. Height is highly heritable, and growth in males typically finishes around 18 to 19.

A 2026 systematic review of 12 studies in children aged 6 months to 12 years found that habitual liquid cow's milk intake was mostly associated with better height, growth velocity or height-for-age scores; experimental studies showed gains in children given milk regularly, while some observational studies found non-significant or adjustment-dependent associations, and one study of complete milk exclusion found slowed linear growth.[5] A 2026 expert review of 70 publications concluded that regular cow's milk supports growth and bone health in healthy children and adolescents, while another 2026 narrative review describes milk as mainly a marker of calcium-rich diets in the bone-mass literature.[12][13] A review of plant-based milk alternatives reported that partly replacing cow's milk with them was linked to slightly lower linear growth, roughly 0.2 cm per daily cup in five-year-olds in the pooled analysis it describes.[14]

All of these studies concern milk as a food group, mostly pasteurised, in children whose diets may otherwise be low in energy or protein. Forum users who discuss the topic frequently point to growth plate fusion as the point after which diet is not expected to change height.[2]

sections.h: Origins: Weston Price, the Primal Diet and the raw-milk movement
paras: Weston A. Price (1870 to 1948) was a Canadian-born, Cleveland-based dentist who chaired the National Dental Association's research body from 1914 to 1928. After years of work on root-canal-treated teeth and focal infection, he turned to nutrition and in 1939 published Nutrition and Physical Degeneration, based on his visits to traditional communities. He argued that refined flour, sugar and modern fats contributed to dental decay, tooth crowding and altered facial development.[7] Reviewers disagreed from the start: a 1940 Canadian Medical Association Journal review praised the book, while others, including a 1981 Nutrition Today editorial, criticised its uncontrolled variables.[7] Looksmaxxing discussions of raw dairy and jaw or midface development draw on this facial-development theme, even though Wikipedia's biography does not tie Price to raw milk specifically.[7]

Aajonus Vonderplanitz (born 1947, died 2013) trademarked the Primal Diet in 2000, centred on raw meat, eggs, dairy and fats, and described it in We Want to Live (1997) and The Recipe for Living Without Disease (2002). He reported high cancer-remission rates among clients but published no case documentation, and his protocols have not been tested by medical researchers.[6] He campaigned for legal raw-milk access in California, helped end Los Angeles County's ban on retail raw-milk sales in 2001, promoted a "private food club" model, and was linked to the Rawesome food club in Los Angeles, whose 2010 and 2011 raids led to charges against associates.[6]

The Weston A. Price Foundation, founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon and Mary Enig, advocates traditional-food diets and legal access to raw milk, and in 2007 helped establish the Farm-to-Consumer Legal Defense Fund.[8] An FDA official quoted in a 2010 Wall Street Journal article described the foundation's raw-milk claims as unsupported by science, and commentators including Quackwatch and Science-Based Medicine have been critical of the foundation.[8] Supporters say these groups defend consumer choice and traditional foods; the Wikipedia raw-milk article also notes that food-freedom advocates frame access as a matter of individual liberty.[9] US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., according to the same article, supports raw milk consumption.[9]

The 2011 meta-analysis in the Journal of Food Protection pooled 40 studies and found that pasteurisation decreased vitamins B1, B2, C and folate, that B12 and E fell and vitamin A rose in qualitative comparisons, and concluded that the effect on milk's nutritive value was minimal; it also examined advocacy claims about allergy, cancer and lactose intolerance.[10] Wikipedia's pasteurisation article adds that milk is a major source of riboflavin (B2) but not of B12 or E in North American diets, so the practical effect varies by vitamin.[15] Wikipedia reports a 2012 Belgian review reaching a similar conclusion and notes the FDA states that pasteurisation does not destroy nutritional value.[9]

Forum posters argue the opposite: one thread claims raw milk keeps vitamins, enzymes and whey protein intact and may support hormones and, in the young, height, and lists as drawbacks a bacterial risk from poor sources and, for some people, acne or bloating.[4]

Studies reporting lower rates of asthma and allergy in farm children are often cited by raw-milk advocates. Wikipedia reports that researchers attribute much of this to broader farm exposure, called the farm effect, rather than to the milk itself.[9] A 2026 umbrella review of 75 risk factors for childhood allergic rhinitis listed raw milk consumption among factors associated with lower risk, while noting that the quality of the underlying evidence was generally low.[16] A trial letter has compared yoghurt with raw milk as an alternative for infant eczema and allergy outcomes.[17] These findings concern allergy, not growth.

A review of raw milk's microbiota lists Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and Campylobacter among the organisms that can occur in it.[18] The CDC lists Campylobacter, Cryptosporidium, E. coli, Listeria, Brucella and Salmonella, names children under five, adults over 65, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems as being at higher risk, and notes that good farm practice can reduce but not eliminate contamination.[11] Wikipedia also lists possible complications such as haemolytic uremic syndrome and Guillain-Barre syndrome.[9] Because the practice is aimed at young people, the CDC's note about higher risk in children is relevant to its target audience.[11]

Wikipedia reports that raw milk was linked to about a quarter of US food and water outbreaks before the Second World War versus under one percent for milk today, that 144 US outbreaks were connected to raw milk between 2007 and 2016, and that from 1998 to 2011 the CDC linked 79 percent of US dairy-related outbreaks to raw milk or raw-milk cheese.[9][15] Not all analysts frame the numbers the same way: a 2024 analysis of US outbreak data for 2005 to 2020 found no evidence of a rising overall burden of infectious foodborne disease and noted that fatal foodborne disease was mostly linked to produce, peanut butter and pasteurised dairy.[19]

Reviews have also described raw-milk transmission of tick-borne encephalitis virus and brucellosis.[20][21] In 2024, after H5N1 avian influenza was detected in US dairy cattle and commercial milk supplies, the FDA advised consumers to avoid raw milk, and Wikipedia notes many cats died after drinking raw milk from infected cows; a Hacker News thread discussed the cat reports.[9][22] The CDC states that drinking raw milk contaminated with live H5N1 to build antibodies is not recommended.[11] A 2026 risk-assessment model estimated much higher per-serving infection probabilities for raw than pasteurised milk and suggested that testing bulk-tank milk lowers raw-milk risk.[23]

Wikipedia reports that about 43 US states permit some form of raw-milk sale, often via farm sales or herdshares, and that the FDA has banned interstate sale for human consumption since 1987.[9] Direct sale is federally prohibited in Canada; about 150 producers in England, Wales and Northern Ireland sell "green top" milk directly; sale for drinking is illegal in Australia, where it is sometimes sold as bath milk; New Zealand and Ireland regulate it; and Catalonia legalised it in 2018.[9] Kenya is cited as a country where most milk is consumed raw.[9]

Looksmax.org threads show both enthusiasm and scepticism. Some members promote raw milk as a looksmax in its own right, others ask whether it is worthwhile, and others discuss where to obtain it.[4][24] The practice is often linked in these threads with raw meat, liver, eggs and carnivore-style eating, and with social-media content from the primal-diet scene.[2][3]

Sceptical posters argue that bone structure is set once growth plates fuse and that raw milk and raw-food diets will not reshape the face; they recommend eating a normal healthy diet and, in the thread's slang, pursuing "hardmaxxing" (surgical or other structural changes) instead.[2] The debate follows a common pattern in looksmaxxing culture, with one group presenting nutrition as a route to better development and another treating skeletal structure as largely fixed by genetics and age.

Humans have drunk milk from domesticated animals since about 9000 to 7000 BC in Mesopotamia, according to Wikipedia's raw milk article, with independent development in the Americas by 3500 to 3000 BC.[9] Louis Pasteur developed pasteurisation in 1864 for wine, Franz von Soxhlet proposed pasteurising milk in 1886, and New York City made milk pasteurisation mandatory in 1910; a 1973 federal rule required pasteurised milk for interstate sale in the US.[15] Before that, tuberculosis from milk is reported to have killed about 65,000 people in England and Wales between 1912 and 1937.[15] In the early twentieth century some US states allowed raw milk certified by medical milk commissions as an alternative to pasteurisation.[9] The modern raw-milk movement emerged in the 1990s and 2000s through the groups described above, and looksmaxxing threads of the mid-2020s tie it to growth and facial development.

The CDC's raw-milk page states that pasteurisation has greatly reduced milk-borne illness since the early 1900s and that pasteurised milk offers the nutritional benefits without raw milk's risks.[11] The FDA and CDC state that pasteurisation does not significantly change milk's nutritional value, and the FDA disputes the claim that pasteurisation destroys beneficial bacteria.[9][8] Advocates respond that regulation limits adult choice and that well-managed farms with testing can produce safe raw milk.

No studies found on raw milk and height. Related research includes systematic reviews of cow's milk and linear growth in children, which are not specific to raw milk, and the 2011 meta-analysis of pasteurisation and vitamin levels, which also assessed advocacy claims about allergy and other outcomes.[10][5] A randomised trial letter examined yoghurt as an alternative to raw milk for infant eczema and allergy, which concerns allergy rather than growth.[17]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, raw milk is debated as a height and bone-structure aid, usually within broader raw-food, primal and carnivore diet discussion.[4][2]
